russland-osteuropa#sections.3.paragraphs: Kievan Rus owed its wealth to trade along the waterway "from the Varangians to the Greeks" via the Dnieper and the Black Sea: furs, wax, honey and slaves went to Byzantium and the Islamic world, while silk, wine and silver came back. Novgorod traded with the Hanseatic League, which kept a trading post there, and supplied furs and wax to the west. Mongol rule destroyed many towns and crafts and burdened the land with tribute for centuries.

In the 16th and 17th centuries Poland-Lithuania became the granary of Europe: nobles had grain grown on their estates by dependent peasants and shipped down the Vistula to Gdańsk and on to the Netherlands. The tsarist empire lived from agriculture, the fur trade from Siberia and later from the iron of the Urals ironworks, which Peter the Great expanded for his fleet and army. In the 18th century Russia was one of the largest iron producers in the world, but much of the work relied on peasants assigned to it by force.

After 1861, and above all from the 1890s, Russia caught up on industrialization with foreign capital and state support under Finance Minister Sergei Witte. Coal and iron from the Donets Basin, oil from Baku and textile mills in Moscow and Łódź grew rapidly, and the Trans-Siberian Railway linked Moscow with the Pacific. Nevertheless the empire remained predominantly agrarian, and peasant yields stayed well below those in Western Europe.
